caveat.headline: Written by this project, not by the town or the district.
caveat.body: Nothing on this page is an official document. These analyses are written here, from documents the town and district published and from records obtained by request. They have not been reviewed or endorsed by the Town of Lunenburg, the Lunenburg School Committee, the Finance Committee or Lunenburg Public Schools, and this project is not affiliated with any of them.
caveat.checkable: Every figure in an analysis is recomputed from the underlying data by a script, and the script is named on the row. The data itself is published below — you do not have to take any of this on trust, and you should not.
caveat.corrections: Where an earlier version of an analysis was wrong, the correction stays in the text rather than being edited out. Several of these documents describe their own earlier errors.

reports.title: FY26, as the books stood in June
reports.about: The school department’s FY26, read line by line from the town’s own ledger. What the $482,101 headline actually is, and three things it cannot explain.

reports.title: FY26 on the town side, as the books stood in June
reports.about: The same ledger read for the other 67 departments. Snow at 292% of its appropriation, a Reserve Fund never touched, and school costs sitting on the town’s books.

reports.title: Budget versus actual
reports.about: Did the money the town budgeted match the money it spent? Careful about what the documents can and cannot support.

reports.title: Free cash: is Lunenburg hoarding, or rebuilding?
reports.about: How much of Lunenburg’s certified free cash is genuinely spendable, built from the state’s own proofs for nine towns.

reports.title: Athletics: what it costs, who pays, and what the budget line does not say
reports.about: The one programme where both sides of the money are visible, and therefore the only place the net-versus-gross problem can be measured rather than described.

reports.title: The athletics ledger: what a fund's cashbook shows that a budget line cannot
reports.about: Three years of the athletics revolving fund at transaction level, from a records request. Includes $254,121.18 described only as “per memo”.

reports.title: Special education and the curve
reports.about: Special education is about 22% of the budget and the largest single driver of the gap. What the rates rest on.

reports.title: Special education, and the money outside the operating budget
reports.about: Whether the special education escalator can be distinguished from grant money unwinding. It currently cannot, and this says why.

reports.title: Lunenburg FY28 — What the source data says (research notes, Aug 2026)
reports.about: What the FY27 budget did, what the override would have done, and what the votes actually decided.

reports.title: Two right numbers
reports.about: Reconciling the district’s published cut list against its own budget columns.

reports.title: What Lunenburg spends for each pupil, and what that number hides
reports.about: What DESE says Lunenburg spends for each pupil, against every district in Massachusetts and against five neighbours — and the arithmetic that says how much of the difference is money and how much is children.

reports.title: What comparable districts actually cut, and in what order
reports.about: What six neighbouring districts did with the same year, and what that does and does not tell you about Lunenburg.

reports.title: Connecting the school budget to the Town's books
reports.about: What can be followed from the school budget to the town’s books, and where it stops. Two levels join, the third cannot, and the format a report arrives in decides which.

reports.title: Show your work
reports.about: Every calculation the site publishes, with its inputs, its formula, a worked example, and whether each figure is published, contractual, statutory, our measurement or our assumption.

reports.title: The Monty Tech assessment — the school bill nobody in Lunenburg votes on
reports.about: The larger of the two routes out of Lunenburg’s own schools, and the only school line the town cannot vote on. What sets the assessment, why 95% of it is a figure the state calculates, and which parts of the twenty-year series are established.

reports.title: A hundred questions this archive can answer
reports.about: The same questions with the query that answers each one, run against the database on every build — so none of them is a claim about what this data can do. If one stops answering, the build fails.

reports.title: What you can ask this archive
reports.about: Every question this archive can answer, in plain English and without a line of SQL. The list a resident should start from: pick the question you actually have and follow it to the figure and the document behind it.

pages.title: The One Big Report
pages.about: Every conclusion this project has reached, read out of the reports that computed them rather than restated here.

pages.title: The blog — one finding at a time, in two minutes
pages.about: Every finding this project has published as a post: the figures, what it means for a resident, a Finance Committee member and a School Committee member, and the links to the report underneath it. About two minutes each.

pages.title: This week in town — meetings coming up, minutes and recordings just posted
pages.about: Meetings coming up for the Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee with what is on each agenda, minutes just posted, recordings just published, and what happened at the last recorded meetings. Refreshed daily.

pages.title: What was said — minutes from the recordings
pages.about: Our minutes of recorded meetings, written from the captions: votes, transfers, budget items, decisions and public comment, every item linked to the video at that second, and checked against the town’s minutes where they exist.

pages.title: Lunenburg by the numbers — who lives here
pages.about: Who lives in Lunenburg — how many people, how old, in how many households, owning or renting, and on what income — from the Census Bureau’s five-year estimates, every figure with its margin of error.

pages.title: Special education — four reports
pages.about: How many Lunenburg children have an individual education programme, from the count DESE publishes rather than from any dollar figure.

pages.title: How many students one special education group may have
pages.about: The state rule everybody argues around, quoted: how many students may be in one special education instructional group, and what staff that takes. With Lunenburg’s own published placement counts beside it, and the reason neither one gives a staffing number.

pages.title: The circuit breaker — what the state reimburses for the costliest placements
pages.about: What the state reimbursed Lunenburg for its costliest special education placements, FY2006 to FY2026, and how the mechanism decides it.

pages.title: What other districts spend, for each pupil
pages.about: What DESE says Lunenburg spends for each pupil — against the districts its own children leave for, against every district in Massachusetts, and against five neighbours — with the arithmetic that says how much of the difference is money and how much is children.

pages.title: What the state requires us to spend — and where that puts us
pages.about: Lunenburg’s net school spending against the minimum Chapter 70 requires, and against every other district in the same year.

pages.title: Chapter 70 — the formula, and why it pays the floor
pages.about: Chapter 70 alone, term by term, out of DESE’s own workbook: what the formula paid Lunenburg each year from FY2007 to FY2026, and why the last four increases are the Legislature’s flat floor rather than anything the formula produced.

pages.title: How Chapter 70 actually works, in eight steps
pages.about: Chapter 70 explained in eight plain steps, in the order the questions actually arrive — what the state prices, what it decides the town can afford, and the one fact everything else follows from: aid is last year’s aid plus an increase, and the increase can be zero.

pages.title: School staffing — did it go up, and over which years
pages.about: Whether school staffing went up — which depends entirely on the years you pick. A window you move yourself, over every year the state has published, and the count of how many spans give each answer.

pages.title: Who works in each school
pages.about: Who the town printed working in each of its four schools, every year from FY2011 — beside the posts and the people the state counts in the same buildings, and why a roster is not a census.

pages.title: The paraprofessionals
pages.about: The biggest single change in who Lunenburg’s schools employ: fewest paraprofessionals per pupil in its comparison group to most, the general education half that grew as the special education half halved, and the budget lines underneath.

pages.title: What courses actually ran, subject by subject
pages.about: How many classes ran in each subject in Lunenburg’s schools, year by year — the one measurement in this archive that counts what was taught rather than who was employed to teach it.

pages.title: The cut register — what was announced, and what shows
pages.about: What Lunenburg’s schools said in writing they were cutting, cycle by cycle, and what an instrument nobody in the argument produced shows afterwards.

pages.title: What stopped being funded
pages.about: Every time a school budget line went to a printed zero, and how many of them came back.

pages.title: When a grant ends — who picks up the bill
pages.about: Every dollar of Lunenburg school spending, split by the fund that paid it, from DESE’s End of Year Financial Report.

pages.title: Who is in the schools — enrolment, FY1994 to today
pages.about: Who is in Lunenburg’s schools: DESE’s headcount, FY1994 to FY2026, by grade band and student group, with the neighbouring districts beside it.

pages.title: Which grades students leave in
pages.about: Which grades Lunenburg children leave in, year by year — DESE’s attrition rate for the district and its schools, SY2010 to SY2026, with every figure kept as the rate it is.

pages.title: Who leaves Lunenburg schools, and where they go
pages.about: Which PUBLIC district educates each of Lunenburg’s resident children, from DESE’s count of residents by district — every public route, both directions, SY2014 onward. Private and parochial schools are not in it.

pages.title: Monty Tech — the assessment, and what sets it
pages.about: What Lunenburg is assessed for Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical, what sets that figure, and what neither the town nor the district publishes about it.

pages.title: If students leave — what school choice would cost
pages.about: What it would cost the town if more children left under school choice — a scenario with dials, priced against DESE’s own counts.

pages.title: What a family actually pays
pages.about: Every school fee a Lunenburg household can be charged, priced for one to four children, and the three places the published record runs out.

pages.title: What sports cost, and who pays
pages.about: Athletics with both sides of the money visible at once — the town’s appropriation, the fee-funded revolving fund, and three district documents that state three different costs for the same team in the same year.

pages.title: Health insurance — the cost outside the school budget
pages.about: School health insurance that is appropriated to a department which is not the schools, with the account number on it.

pages.title: Budgets against what was later reported
pages.about: What the district budgeted against what it later reported spending, line by line — and why nothing before FY2026 is an accounting record.

database.about: Every figure on this site in one SQLite file. The same database the analyses are computed from.

api.about: A read-only JSON API. No key, no rate limit. /api/schema states the grain of each table and the four ways to get a confident wrong answer out of it.

sources.about: Every source document, with its address, the publisher’s own filename and a checksum.

grossBudget.about: The district’s budget in the district’s own shape, with what was actually spent and what other money paid for it — and amber cells wherever that money is not held.
